clinicalPearls: Hymenolepis nana, the dwarf tapeworm, is the most common human tapeworm worldwide and predominates in children in warm climates with crowding and poor sanitation
Uniquely among human tapeworms it can complete its entire life cycle within one host and does not require an intermediate host, so eggs passed in stool are directly infective to humans
This capacity for internal autoinfection allows worm numbers to build up markedly, and heavy burdens produce abdominal pain, diarrhoea, anorexia and, in children, irritability and weight loss
Light infections are usually asymptomatic and detected incidentally on stool examination
Diagnosis is by finding the characteristic eggs, which have an inner envelope with polar thickenings bearing filaments, on stool microscopy
Immunosuppression can permit unusually heavy or persistent infection
Praziquantel is the treatment of choice and is more effective than older agents against this cestode, with attention to hygiene to limit reinfection
reference.pathophysiology: Hymenolepis nana is distinctive because it can complete its cycle entirely within the human intestine. Ingested eggs, or eggs released internally from mature proglottids, hatch and the oncosphere penetrates an intestinal villus to develop into a cysticercoid larva, which then re-enters the lumen and matures into an adult attached to the mucosa. This internal autoinfection lets the worm population expand within a single host without any intermediate stage, so heavy burdens can accumulate, particularly where reinfection from the environment is also ongoing. Mucosal irritation and the metabolic burden of numerous worms underlie the abdominal symptoms and, in children with heavy infection, poor weight gain, while the direct faecal-oral infectivity of the eggs accounts for ready spread in crowded settings.
additionalDifferentials: Other tapeworm infections such as taeniasis and diphyllobothriasis
Other causes of childhood failure to thrive
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for characteristic eggs with polar filaments
Stool concentration methods to improve detection
Repeated sampling in light or intermittent infection
Full blood count including eosinophil count
Assessment of growth and nutritional status in children
Consideration of immune status where infection is unusually heavy or persistent
redFlags: Heavy symptomatic infection with weight loss in a child
Unusually severe or persistent infection suggesting immunosuppression
Failure to clear infection due to ongoing autoinfection or reinfection
reference.prognosis: Good; infection responds well to praziquantel, though autoinfection and environmental reinfection can cause persistence or relapse unless treatment and hygiene measures are adequate.
pitfalls: Underestimating the role of internal autoinfection in perpetuating heavy infection
Using less effective older anthelmintics rather than praziquantel
Neglecting hygiene and contact measures, allowing reinfection
Overlooking immunosuppression in unusually heavy or refractory cases
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
